extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly, historical-philosophical exposition analysing Zeno's paradoxes of motion and Plato's philosophy of mathematics, focusing on underlying hypotheses (continuity vs. indivisibles), methods (geometric/dialectic), and what counts as valid mathematical explanation or refutation. Useful for understanding criteria for mathematical rigor, method, and interpretation of ancient arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis of infinite divisibility (first two arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and second arguments proceed on the hypothesis that continuous magnitudes are divisible ad infinitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or reconstructing the Dichotomy and Achilles, identify and make explicit the assumption of infinite divisibility of space/time; the paradoxes derive their force from this hypothesis. Any attempted refutation must address how the endless series of subdivisions can be exhausted or shown harmless (e.g., Cantor's theory of continuity or limit arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis of indivisible elements (last two arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The last two [arguments] appear to proceed on the opposite hypothesis that space and time are not infinitely divisible, but that they are composed of indivisible elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the Arrow and the Stadium, check whether the argument assumes time/space are made of indivisible instants/atoms; exposing this assumption shows the paradox arises from treating instants as absolute indivisible units. Evaluations should test this premise and its consequences (e.g., instant-as-atom leads to contradictions about occupying two positions in one instant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'how' from 'when' in refutation
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that the sum of the infinite series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... equals 2, or to calculate the exact moment when Achilles will overtake the tortoise, is to answer the question 'when?', whereas the question actually asked is 'how?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct refutation must address the same question the paradox poses. Mathematical calculation of limits answers when an event occurs but may not address the explanatory 'how' of traversing an infinite regress. Be explicit which question your method answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat infinite regress as needing 'harmlessness' proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeno's argument has then to be met by proving that the 'infinite regress' in this case is 'harmless'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronting regress-based paradoxes, one must show that the regress does not prevent the purported phenomenon (e.g., motion) — e.g., by demonstrating convergence, existence of limits, or another principled account that renders the infinite sequence non-obstructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't conflate relative and absolute motion (Stadium fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy of the reasoning [in the Stadium] lies in the assumption that an equal magnitude occupies an equal time in passing with equal velocity a magnitude that is in motion and a magnitude that is at rest, an assumption which is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that time taken to pass a given spatial magnitude is the same in cases of absolute vs. relative motion. Carefully distinguish frames of reference and relations between moving and stationary magnitudes when comparing durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Arrow: treatment of instants and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: If everything is either at rest or moving when it occupies a space equal (to itself), while the object moved is always in the instant ... the moving arrow is unmoved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the Arrow argument by examining whether time is being modelled as composed of indivisible instants; if instants are indivisible, change of position within an instant is impossible, so the argument follows. But denying instants as indivisible (Aristotle's reply) dissolves the paradox. Be explicit about your temporal ontology when reasoning about instantaneous states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Static theory of variables / rejection of infinitesimals
rubrics_metrics.description: Every possible value of a variable is a constant ... When once it is firmly realized that all the values of a variable are constants, it becomes easy to see ... that there are no infinitesimal differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysing continua and motion, one can adopt a 'static' view: treat values as definite constants and use limits to avoid infinitesimals. This guides modern refutations of Zeno by removing infinitesimal quantities as ontologically primitive and modelling velocity/derivative as limit concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass/Russell view: motion as occupation of places at times
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion consists merely in the occupation of different places at different times, subject to continuity ... There is no transition from place to place, no consecutive moment or consecutive position, no such thing as velocity except in the sense of a real number which is the limit of a certain set of quotients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalising motion, use epsilon-delta/limit definitions: velocity and acceleration are not instantaneous physical states but limit values. This mathematical stance dissolves paradoxes that rely on instantaneous 'states of motion' as physical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evade Zeno by simultaneous divisibility claim
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an answer to say that the two series [space and time] are exhausted simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject simplistic replies that assert both time and space are infinitely divisible and so 'both exhausted together' — the explanatory problem remains. A satisfactory account must explain how an actual traversal of infinitely many subdivisions can occur (e.g., via convergence/limit processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the foundational hypothesis before critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The connexion between the arguments against the Many and those against motion lies in the fact that the former rest on the assumption of the divisibility of bodies ad infinitum; assuming this, he easily proved ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before critiquing a philosophical or mathematical argument, identify the foundational metaphysical/mathematical hypotheses (e.g., divisibility, indivisibles, nature of instants). Many apparent contradictions are consequences of unexamined background assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of mathematics (Plato): training of the mind, not utility
rubrics_metrics.description: What Plato emphasizes throughout when speaking of mathematics is its value for the training of the mind; its practical utility is of no account in comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging mathematical work (per Platonic standard), prioritize the capacity of mathematical study to cultivate intellect and grasp eternal truths over immediate practical applicability. Present arguments accordingly if appealing to Platonic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: True astronomy/harmonics as idealized, not observational
rubrics_metrics.description: True astronomy is ... a kind of ideal kinematics, dealing with the laws of motion of true stars in a sort of mathematical heaven ... The true science of harmonics should be altogether independent of observation and experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess theories by their abstraction to ideal forms: observational irregularities are treated as imperfect illustrations or problems leading to ideal, mathematical models. Distinguish between empirical practice and the ideal theory intended to capture essential relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry's essence: study of eternal mathematical objects, not constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of geometry is therefore directly opposed even to the language which, for want of better terms, geometers are obliged to use ... Constructions, then, or the processes of squaring, adding, and so on, are not of the essence of geometry, but are actually antagonistic to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value proofs and reasoning about ideal objects (points, lines, triangles) over mechanical constructions; treat diagrams as illustrative aids rather than constitutive of geometric truth. When evaluating geometric work, distinguish theoretical insight from instrumental/constructive technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical hypotheses as starting points
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who occupy themselves with geometries and calculations ... take for granted the odd and the even, figures, three kinds of angles, and other things cognate to these in each subject; assuming these things as known, they take them as hypotheses ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and state explicitly the hypotheses (axioms, definitions) underlying a mathematical development. Treat them as agreed starting points for arguments, but be aware of their role and limits; do not mistake them for ultimate principles without further justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two intellectual methods: geometric (hypothesis-as-principle) vs. dialectic (hypothesis-as-step)
rubrics_metrics.description: The one method cannot get above these hypotheses, but, treating them as if they were first principles, builds upon them ... The other method treats the hypotheses as being really hypotheses and nothing more, but uses them as stepping-stones for mounting higher and higher until the principle of all things is reached ... this method is the dialectical method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating mathematical/philosophical work, be explicit which method is used: constructive/deductive mathematics (accepting hypotheses) or dialectical/analytic ascent (seeking non-hypothetical first principles). For foundational claims, prefer dialectical analysis to justify or replace hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic and division methods for discovery and demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest is the method which by means of analysis carries the thing sought up to an acknowledged principle ... The second is the method of division, which divides into its parts the genus proposed for consideration ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mathematical discovery and exposition, employ analysis (working backwards from the goal to known principles) and division (taxonomic decomposition of genera into species) as systematic methods to reach proofs or to found demonstrations on acknowledged principles.
